title: Development cooperation is being judged by country ownership, results, inclusion, transparency, and mutual accountability rather than financial volume alone
source_unit: OECD-UNDP, Making Development Co-operation More Effective: Progress Report 2026
geography: Global development-cooperation partnerships reporting across partner-country governments, development partners, civil society, trade unions, and private-sector representatives

denominator.unit: partner-country governments reporting in the monitoring round

partner_count.unit: development partners reporting in the monitoring round

stakeholder_scope.value: Civil-society organizations, trade unions, and private-sector representatives also contributed to the monitoring round

observations.method: Global Partnership monitoring round summarized by OECD and UNDP using reporting from partner-country governments, development partners, civil society, trade unions, and private-sector representatives.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary establishes reporting participation and the monitoring scope but does not by itself show response completeness, indicator-level results, causal effects, or representativeness of all development cooperation.
observations.subgroup: Partner-country governments, ministries, local institutions, development partners, civil society, trade unions, private firms, and communities affected by development programs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad reporting participation can improve accountability while still favoring institutions with data capacity and leaving informal, marginalized, or politically weaker actors underrepresented.

ownership.value: Country ownership is treated as a core condition of more effective development cooperation

results.value: The agenda emphasizes focus on results rather than inputs or announcements alone

partnership_quality.value: Inclusive partnerships, transparency, and mutual accountability are presented as central dimensions of cooperation quality

observations.method: OECD-UNDP progress synthesis of the Global Partnership monitoring round and its aid-effectiveness agenda.
observations.uncertainty: Normative principles do not demonstrate that country ownership is real, that results are attributable to cooperation, or that transparency and accountability are distributed equally across partners.
observations.subgroup: Government ministries, local authorities, civil society, workers, firms, donors, implementing agencies, and intended program beneficiaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Country ownership can improve fit and legitimacy, but governments themselves may not represent all affected groups; strong results frameworks can also privilege measurable outputs over cultural, political, or relational value.

diagnostic_function.value: The report provides a snapshot of progress, challenges, and emerging opportunities in making development cooperation more effective

action_route.value: It aims to move from evidence to jointly agreed action among partner-country governments and their partners

development_link.value: The stated purpose is to strengthen partnership quality and accelerate progress toward the 2030 Agenda and SDGs

observations.method: Progress report translating monitoring evidence into a shared action agenda for development-cooperation actors.
observations.uncertainty: A shared action agenda does not establish agreement on priorities, financing, implementation authority, or whether changes will improve outcomes for affected populations.
observations.subgroup: Governments, development partners, civil society, trade unions, private-sector actors, implementing organizations, and communities seeking influence over development choices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Joint action can reduce fragmentation, but consensus-oriented processes can also smooth over power asymmetries, conflict, and disagreement about whose definition of results should prevail.

institutional_route.value: Development cooperation is framed as a relationship among national institutions, external partners, civil society, workers, and firms rather than a one-way donor transfer

accountability_route.value: Transparency and mutual accountability are intended to make commitments, implementation, and results visible across partners

system_condition.value: The report treats partnership quality and institutional coordination as conditions for accelerating sustainable development

observations.method: OECD-UNDP institutional synthesis of development-cooperation monitoring and partnership practices.
observations.uncertainty: The cooperation frame does not measure bargaining power, resource control, local implementation capacity, or downstream changes in household, worker, or community outcomes.
observations.subgroup: National and local governments, donors, multilateral institutions, workers, civil society, private firms, and populations receiving or affected by development investments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Multi-actor governance can surface knowledge and improve coordination, but it may also increase transaction costs and create accountability gaps when responsibility is distributed across many organizations.

boundary: This record adds a development-cooperation governance signal linking country ownership, results, inclusive partnerships, transparency, mutual accountability, institutional coordination, and implementation. It is a progress-monitoring and policy report, not a respondent-level dataset, causal impact evaluation, complete aid inventory, or proof that shared action improves realized outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNDP publication page reviewed for publication date, 2023–2026 monitoring round, 44 partner-country governments, 93 development partners, stakeholder scope, country ownership, results, inclusive partnerships, transparency, mutual accountability, and evidence-to-action framing.
